L146: 【76†Anatomical terminology】
L147: The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) is one of a pair of 【77†cerebral arteries】 that supplies oxygenated blood to most midline portions of the 【78†frontal lobes】 and 【79†superior medial parietal】 【80†lobes of the brain】. The two anterior cerebral arteries arise from the 【64†internal carotid artery】 and are part of the 【81†circle of Willis】. The left and right anterior cerebral arteries are connected by the 【82†anterior communicating artery】.
L148: 【83†Anterior cerebral artery syndrome】 refers to symptoms that follow a 【84†stroke】 occurring in the area normally supplied by one of the arteries. It is characterized by 【85†weakness】 and sensory loss in the lower leg and foot opposite to the lesion and behavioral changes.
L149: ## Structure
L150: 
L151: [【86†edit】]
L152: 
L153: Arteries of the brain. Anterior cerebral artery labeled at the left (twice)
L154: 
L155: The anterior cerebral artery is divided into 5 segments. Its smaller branches: the callosal (supracallosal) arteries are considered to be the A4 and A5 segments.^{【87†[1]】}^{【88†[2]】}
L156:   * A1 originates from the internal carotid artery and extends to the anterior communicating artery (AComm). The anteromedial central (medial lenticulostriate) arteries arise from this segment as well as the AComm, which irrigates the 【89†caudate nucleus】 and the anterior limb of the 【90†internal capsule】
L157:   * A2 extends from the AComm to the bifurcation forming the pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries. The 【91†recurrent artery of Heubner】 (distal medial striate artery), which irrigates the internal capsule, usually arises at the beginning of this segment near the AComm. Two branches arise from this segment:
L158:     * Orbitofrontal artery (medial frontal basal): Arises a small distance away from the AComm
L159:     * Frontopolar artery (polar frontal): Arises after the orbitofrontal, close to the curvature of A2 over the 【92†corpus callosum】. It can also originate from the callosal marginal.
L160:   * A3, also termed the pericallosal artery, is one of the (or the only) main terminal branches of the ACA, which extends posteriorly in the pericallosal sulcus to form the internal parietal arteries (superior, inferior) and the precuneal artery. This artery may form an 【93†anastomosis】 with the 【94†posterior cerebral artery】.
L161:     * Callosal marginal artery: A commonly present terminal branch of the ACA, which bifurcates from the pericallosal artery. This artery in turn branches into the medial frontal arteries (anterior, intermediate, posterior), and the paracentral artery, with the 【95†cingulate】 branches arising throughout its length. Depending on 【96†anatomical variation】, the callosal marginal artery may be none discrete or not be visible.
L162: In the latter case, the branches mentioned will originate from the pericallosal artery. In a study of 76 hemispheres, the artery was present in only 60% of the cases.^{【97†[3]】} Angiography studies cite that the vessel can be seen 67% ^{【87†[1]】} or 50%^{【98†[4]】} of the time.

L127: 【57†Anatomical terminology】
L128: In 【58†human anatomy】, the anterior communicating artery is a 【59†blood vessel】 of the 【60†brain】 that connects the left and right 【50†anterior cerebral arteries】.
L129: ## Anatomy
L130: 
L131: [【61†edit】]
L132: 
L133: The anterior communicating artery connects the two anterior cerebral arteries across the commencement of the 【62†longitudinal fissure】. Sometimes this vessel is wanting, the two arteries joining to form a single trunk, which afterward divides; or it may be wholly, or partially, divided into two. Its length averages about 4 mm, but varies greatly. It gives off some of the anteromedial ganglionic vessels, but these are principally derived from the anterior cerebral artery.
L134: It is part of the 【63†cerebral arterial circle】, also known as the 【63†circle of Willis】.^{【64†[1]】}
L135: ## Physiology
L136: 
L137: [【65†edit】]
L138: 
L139: Anatomical variations of the anterior communicating artery are relatively common. The artery is sometimes duplicated, multiplicated, fenestrated ("net-like") or very short, giving the impression that two anterior cerebral arteries are fused at the point where the anterior communicating artery is usually expected to arise.^{【66†[2]】}
L140: Normally, the anterior communicating artery does not significantly contribute to cerebral blood supply, as there is negligible net blood flow within it, and some of its anteromedial branches seem to be specially adapted to ease forebrain sodium sensing, rather than to supply the brain with blood.^{【67†[3]】}
L141: ## Pathology
L142: 
L143: [【68†edit】]
L144: 
L145: 【69†Aneurysms】 of the anterior communicating artery are the most common circle of Willis aneurysm^{【70†[4]】} and can cause 【71†visual field defects】 such as 【72†bitemporal heteronymous hemianopsia】 (due to compression of the 【73†optic chiasm】),^{【74†[5]】} 【75†psychopathology】 and 【76†frontal lobe】 pathology.^{【77†[6]】}
L146: In case of narrowing of other arteries of the circle of Willis or the arteries supplying the circle, the anterior communicating artery can provide a way to supply blood to the opposite (affected) side of the circle. This can often preserve the cerebral blood supply well enough to avoid the symptoms of 【78†ischemia】.^{【79†[7]】}
L147: The arteries of the base of the brain. Anterior communicating artery at top. The 【80†temporal】 pole of the 【81†cerebrum】 and a portion of the 【82†cerebellar】 hemisphere have been removed on the right side. Inferior aspect (viewed from below).

L116: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
L117: ---

L132: 【63†Anatomical terminology】
L133: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) is one of three pairs of 【64†arteries】 that supplies blood to the 【55†cerebellum】.
L134: It arises from the 【51†basilar artery】 on each side at the level of the junction between the 【65†medulla oblongata】 and the 【56†pons】 in the 【66†brainstem】. It has a variable course, passing backward to be distributed to the anterior part of the undersurface of the cerebellum, 【67†anastomosing】 with both the 【50†posterior inferior cerebellar】 (PICA) branch of the 【68†vertebral artery】 and the 【49†superior cerebellar artery】.
L135: It also gives off the internal auditory or 【52†labyrinthine artery】 in most cases; however, the labyrinthine artery can less commonly emerge as a branch of the 【51†basilar artery】.
L136: 
L137: The amount of tissue receiving blood supply from the AICA is variable, depending upon whether the PICA is more or less dominant, but usually includes the anteroinferior surface of the 【55†cerebellum】, the 【69†flocculus】, 【70†middle cerebellar peduncle】 and inferolateral portion of the pons.^{【71†[1]】}
L138: ## Clinical significance
L139: 
L140: [【72†edit】]
L141: Occlusion of AICA is considered rare, but generally results in a 【73†lateral pontine syndrome】, also known as AICA syndrome.
L142: The symptoms include sudden onset of 【74†vertigo】, vomiting, 【75†nystagmus】, 【76†dysarthria】, falling to the side of the lesion (due to damage to 【77†vestibular nuclei】), and a variety of same-side features including 【78†hemiataxia】, loss of all types of sensation of the face (due to damage to the 【79†principal sensory trigeminal nucleus】), facial paralysis (due to damage to the 【80†facial nucleus】), and hearing loss and 【81†tinnitus】 (due to damage to the 【82†cochlear nuclei】).^{【83†[2]】}^{【84†[3]】}^{【85†[4]】} Facial nucleus damage and its resulting paralysis are specific to AICA lesions, and may be the most distinct clinical identifier of this type of stroke before a 【86†CT scan】 or 【87†MRI】 may be obtained.^{【88†[5]】}
L143: Vertigo may sometimes present as an isolated symptom several weeks or months before acute ischemia and cerebral infarction occurs, probably with the meaning of transient ischemia of the inner ear or the 【89†vestibular nerve】.^{【90†[6]】}
L144: There is also loss of pain and temperature sensation from the contralateral (opposite-side) limbs and trunk, which can lead to diagnostic confusion with 【91†lateral medullary syndrome】, which also gives rise to "crossed" neurological signs but does not normally cause 【92†cochlear】 symptoms, severe facial palsy or broad facial sensory loss.^{【93†[7]】}

L122: Anterior spinal artery
L123: ---

L132: Details
L133: ---
L134: Source  | 【63†Vertebral arteries】
L135: 【64†Vein】  | 【58†Anterior spinal veins】
L136: Identifiers
L137: ---
L138: 【65†Latin】  | arteria spinalis anterior
L139: 【66†TA98】  | 【67†A12.2.08.016†ifaa.unifr.ch】
L140: 【66†TA2】  | 【68†4525†ta2viewer.openanatomy.org】

L142: 【71†Anatomical terminology】
L143: In 【72†human anatomy】, the anterior spinal artery is the 【73†artery】 that supplies the anterior portion of the 【74†spinal cord】. It arises from branches of the 【63†vertebral arteries】 and courses along the anterior aspect of the spinal cord. It is reinforced by several contributory arteries, especially the 【75†artery of Adamkiewicz】.
L144: ## Anatomy
L145: 
L146: [【76†edit】]
L147: 
L148: ### Origin
L149: 
L150: [【77†edit】]
L151: 
L152: The anterior spinal artery typically arises bilaterally as two small branches near the termination of the 【63†vertebral arteries】.^{【78†[1]】}
L153: ### Course
L154: 
L155: [【79†edit】]
L156: 
L157: Descending in front of the 【80†medulla oblongata】, they unite at the level of the 【81†foramen magnum】. The single trunk descends in the front of the 【82†medulla spinalis】, extending to the lowest part of the medulla spinalis. It is continued as a slender twig on the 【83†filum terminale】. The vessel passes in the 【84†pia mater】 along the 【85†anterior median fissure】.
L158: ### Branches
L159: 
L160: [【86†edit】]
L161: On its course the artery takes several small branches (i.e. 【62†anterior segmental medullary arteries】), which enter the 【87†vertebral canal】 through the 【88†intervertebral foramina】.
L162: These branches are derived from the 【63†vertebral artery】, the 【89†ascending cervical artery】, a branch of the 【90†inferior thyroid artery】 in the neck, the 【91†intercostal arteries】 in the 【92†thorax】, and from the 【93†lumbar artery】, 【94†iliolumbar artery】 and 【95†lateral sacral arteries】 in the 【96†abdomen】 and 【97†pelvis】.
L163: ### Distribution
L164: 
L165: [【98†edit】]
L166: 
L167: It supplies the pia mater, and the substance of the medulla spinalis, also sending off branches at its lower part to be distributed to the 【99†cauda equina】.
L168: ## Disorders
L169: 
L170: [【100†edit】]
L171: Disruption of the anterior spinal artery leads to bilateral disruption of the 【101†corticospinal tract】, causing motor deficits, and bilateral disruption of the 【102†spinothalamic tract】, causing sensory deficits in the form of pain/temperature sense loss. It is called 【103†anterior spinal artery syndrome】. This occurs when the disruption of the anterior spinal artery is at the level of the spinal cord.
L172: Contrast this with 【104†medial medullary syndrome】, when the anterior spinal artery is occluded at the level of the 【80†medulla oblongata】.
L173: Disruption of its perforating branches (sulcal artery) can result in a hemicord syndrome. In fact, acute sulcal artery syndrome should be suspected in patients with acute hemicord syndrome, and vertebral artery dissection should be suspected in cases of high cervical cord involvement. In a recent review by Tan YJ, et al. in 2021, good functional recovery was seen in most, and vertebral artery dissection was the leading cause of sulcal artery syndrome.^{【105†[2]】}

L117: Anterior choroidal artery
L118: ---
L119: Diagram of the arterial circulation at the base of the brain (inferior view). The anterior choroidal artery is labeled at right of the 【49†circle of Willis】.
L120: Details
L121: ---
L122: Source  | 【50†Internal carotid artery】
L123: Identifiers
L124: ---
L125: 【51†Latin】  | arteria choroidea anterior
L126: 【52†TA98】  | 【53†A12.2.06.019†ifaa.unifr.ch】
L127: 【52†TA2】  | 【54†4501†ta2viewer.openanatomy.org】
L128: 【55†FMA】  | 【56†50087†bioportal.bioontology.org】
L129: 【57†Anatomical terminology】
L130: The anterior choroidal artery is a 【58†bilaterally paired】 artery of the brain. It is typically a branch of the 【50†internal carotid artery】 which supplies the 【59†choroid plexus】 of 【60†lateral ventricle】 and 【61†third ventricle】 as well as numerous structures of the brain.
L131: 
L132: Occlusion of the artery can result in loss of sensation, loss of part of the 【62†visual field】, and impaired movement, all on the opposite side of the body as the occlusion.
L133: ## Structure
L134: 
L135: [【63†edit】]
L136: 
L137: ### Origin
L138: 
L139: [【64†edit】]
L140: 
L141: The anterior choroidal artery typically originates from the 【50†internal carotid artery】. It may (rarely) instead arise from the 【65†middle cerebral artery】.^{【66†[1]】}
L142: 
L143: It originates from the distal 【50†internal carotid artery (ICA)】 5 mm distal to the origin of the 【67†posterior communicating artery】 and just proximal to the terminal bifurcation of the ICA.^{【68†[2]】}
L144: ### Course
L145: 
L146: [【69†edit】]
L147: It initially course posterolaterally on the inferior surface of the cerebral hemisphere alongside the optic tract, crossing the tract medial-to-lateral^{【70†[3]】} inferior to the tract.^{【71†[4]】} At the level of the 【72†lateral geniculate nucleus】, it curves around the lateral aspect of the 【73†cerebral peduncle】 to reach its posterior aspect.
L148: It reaches the medial portion of the 【74†transverse cerebral fissure】 to enter the lateral ventricle.^{【70†[3]】} It enters the lateral ventricle at the apex of its 【75†inferior horn】, at the inferior extremity of choroid fissure, just superior to the 【76†uncus】.^{【71†[4]】}
L149: ### Distribution
L150: 
L151: [【77†edit】]
L152: 
L153: It serves structures in the prosencephalon, diencephalon, and mesencephalon:^{【68†[2]】}
L154:   * 【59†choroid plexus】 of the 【60†lateral ventricle】 and 【61†third ventricle】
L155:   * 【78†optic chiasm】 and 【79†optic tract】
L156:   * (genu, posterior limb, and retrolentiform part of^{【70†[3]】}) 【80†internal capsule】
L157:   * 【81†lateral geniculate body】
L158:   * 【82†globus pallidus】
L159:   * tail of the 【83†caudate nucleus】
L160:   * (【84†tuber cinereum】 of^{【70†[3]】}) 【85†hippocampus】
L161:   * 【86†amygdala】
L162:   * 【87†substantia nigra】
L163:   * 【88†red nucleus】
L164:   * 【89†crus cerebri】
L165: ## Clinical significance
L166: 
L167: [【90†edit】]
L168: Occlusion of the artery results in 【91†contralateral】 【92†hemianopsia】 (partial loss of vision) and hemianaesthesia (loss of sensation), as well as partial 【93†hemiplegia】 (loss of the ability to move).^{【71†[4]】} These symptoms are thought to arise from 【94†ischemic】 damage to the posterior limb of the 【80†internal capsule】, 【95†thalamus】, and 【78†optic chiasm】/【79†optic tract】.
L169: However, the posterior limb of the internal capsule also receives lenticulostriate arteries from the 【65†middle cerebral artery】, thus creating partially redundant supply.^{【96†[5]】}

L149: 【80†Anatomical terminology】
L150: The middle cerebral artery (MCA) is one of the three major paired 【81†cerebral arteries】 that supply 【82†blood】 to the 【71†cerebrum】. The MCA arises from the 【83†internal carotid artery】 and continues into the 【84†lateral sulcus】 where it then branches and projects to many parts of the lateral 【85†cerebral cortex】. It also supplies blood to the anterior 【86†temporal lobes】 and the 【87†insular cortices】.
L151: The left and right MCAs rise from trifurcations of the 【83†internal carotid arteries】 and thus are connected to the 【88†anterior cerebral arteries】 and the 【89†posterior communicating arteries】, which connect to the 【90†posterior cerebral arteries】. The MCAs are not considered a part of the 【66†Circle of Willis】.^{【91†[1]】}
L152: ## Structure
L153: 
L154: [【92†edit】]
L155: 
L156: Middle cerebral artery Middle cerebral artery and its branches (patient has a hypoplastic A1 segment and an absent PCOM, resulting in a purely MCA angio from internal carotid artery injection)
L157: 
L158: The middle cerebral artery divides into four segments, named by the region they supply as opposed to order of branching as the latter can be somewhat variable:^{【93†[2]】}
L159:   * M1: The sphenoidal segment (stem),^{【94†[3]】} receiving its name due to its course along the adjacent 【95†sphenoid bone】. It is also referred to as the horizontal segment, though this may be misleading since the segment may descend, remain flat, or extend posteriorly the anterior (dorsad) in different individuals. The M1 segment perforates the brain with numerous 【68†anterolateral central】 (lateral lenticulostriate) arteries, which supply the 【96†basal ganglia】.
L160:   * M2: Extending anteriorly on the 【87†insula】, this segment is known as the insular segment. It is also known as the Sylvian segment when the 【97†opercular】 segments are included. The MCA branches may bifurcate or sometimes trifurcate into trunks in this segment which then extend into branches that terminate towards the cortex.
L161:   * M3: The opercular segment, extending laterally and exteriorly from the insula towards the cortex. This segment is sometimes grouped with M2.
L162:   * M4: These finer terminal or cortical segments irrigate the cortex. They begin at the external margins of the Sylvian fissure and extend distally away on the cortex of the brain.
L163: The M2 and M3 segments may each split into 2 or 3 main trunks (terminal branches) with an upper trunk, lower trunk and occasionally a middle trunk. Bifurcations and trifurcations occurs in 50% and 25% of the cases respectively.
L164: Other cases include duplication of the MCA at the 【83†internal carotid artery】 (ICA) or an accessory MCA (AccMCA) which arise not from the ICA but as a branch from the anterior cerebral artery.^{【98†[4]】} The middle trunk that exist in parts of the population, when present provides the pre-Rolandic, Rolandic, anterior parietal, posterior parietal and the angular artery for irrigation instead of the upper and lower trunks.
L165: The branches of the MCA can be described by the areas that they irrigate.
L166: ### Frontal lobe
L167: 
L168: [【99†edit】]
L169:   * Lateral frontobasal (orbitiofrontal): This artery branches out anteriorly, superiorly and laterally to vascularize the inferior frontal gyrus. It "competes" in size with the frontal polar branch of the 【88†anterior cerebral artery】
L170:   * Prefrontal arteries: These arteries fan out over the insula and exit to the cortex via the medial surface of the frontal 【97†operculum】. The arteries fan superiorly over the 【100†pars triangularis】 and vascularize the inferior and middle frontal gyrus. Near the superior frontal gyrus these arteries 【101†anastomose】 with branches from the pericallosal artery of the anterior cerebral artery.
L171:   * Pre-Rolandic artery (precentral): The artery extends out on the medial surface of the operculum and supplies the posterior parts of the middle and inferior frontal gyri as well as the lower parts of the pre-central gyrus. This artery branches once or twice and is relatively invariant across anatomies.
L172:   * Rolandic arteries (central): The artery extends out and exits from the central portion of the operculum then passes inside the central sulcus. This artery bifurcates in 72% of individuals and irrigates the posterior pre-central gyrus and the inferior portion of the post-central gyrus.
L173: ### Parietal lobe
L174: 
L175: [【102†edit】]
L176:   * Anterior parietal: This artery usually originates from a distal MCA branch. In some cases it branches from the rolandic artery or from the posterior parietal artery. It extends the length of interparietal sulcus and descends slightly posteriorly.
L177:   * Posterior parietal: Emerges from the posterior end of the Sylvian fissure and extends first posteriorly, and then anteriorly along the posterior of the parietal lobe. It also branches to the supramarginal gyrus.
L178:   * Angular: The angular artery is a significant terminal branch of the anterior or middle trunk of the MCA. It emerges from the Sylvian fissure and passes over the anterior transverse temporal gyrus and usually divides into two branches. One of the branches supplies the 【103†angular gyrus】 while the other supplies the supramarginal gyrus, posterior superior temporal gyrus, and the parietooccipital arcus (sulcus).
L179:   * Temporooccipital: The longest cortical artery, it runs posteriorly opposite to the center of the operculum. Upon its exit from the Sylvian fissure, it runs parallel to the superior temporal sulcus and supplies the superior and inferior occipital gyri. This vessel anastamoses with the posterior cerebral artery and may exist as one or two arteries, 67% or 33% of the time, respectively.
L180: ### Temporal lobe
L181: 
L182: [【104†edit】]
L183:   * Temporopolar: The artery extends from the sphenoidal segment of the MCA via the inferior surface of the operculum and supplies the polar and anterior lateral portions of the temporal lobe. The vessel can be identified in 52% of normal angiograms
L184:   * Anterior temporal: This artery typically arises from the proximal MCA trunk and extends in the similar fashion as the temporopolar artery and vascularizes the same regions.
L185:   * Middle temporal: This artery extends from the Sylvian fissure opposite to the inferior frontal gyrus and supplies superior and middle portions of the middle temporal lobe. It can be identified in 79% of angiograms.
L186:   * Posterior temporal: This artery extends out and away from the operculum and turns in a step-wise manner first inferiorly then posteriorly into the superior temporal sulcus then to the middle temporal sulcus. This vessel supplies posterior portion of the temporal lobe and is the origin of several perforating arteries that irrigate the insula. It is readily identifiable in most radiograms.
L187: ## Function
L188: 
L189: [【105†edit】]
L190: 
L191: Areas supplied by the middle cerebral artery include:
L192:   * The bulk of the lateral surface of the hemisphere; except for the superior inch of the frontal and 【106†parietal lobe】 (【88†anterior cerebral artery】), and the inferior part of the 【86†temporal lobe】.
L193:   * Superior division supplies lateroinferior frontal lobe (location of 【107†Broca's area】 i.e. language expression)
L194:   * Inferior division supplies lateral temporal lobe (location of 【108†Wernicke's area】 i.e. language comprehension)
L195:   * Deep branches supply the 【96†basal ganglia】 as well as the 【109†internal capsule】
L196: MCA occlusion site and resulting Aphasia
L197: 
L198:   * Global – trunk of MCA
L199:   * Broca – anterior branch of MCA
L200:   * Wernicke – posterior branch of MCA
L201: ## Clinical significance
L202: 
L203: [【110†edit】]
L204: ### Occlusion
L205: 
L206: [【111†edit】]
L207: 
L208: Main article: 【112†Middle cerebral artery syndrome】
L209: 
L210: 【113†Occlusion】 of the middle cerebral artery results in 【112†Middle cerebral artery syndrome】, potentially showing the following defects:
L211:   1. 【114†Paralysis】 (-plegia) or weakness (-paresis) of the contralateral face and arm (faciobrachial)
L212:   2. Sensory loss of the contralateral face and arm.
L213:   3. Damage to the dominant hemisphere (usually the left hemisphere) results in aphasia (i.e. 【107†Broca's area】 or 【115†Wernicke's】)
L214:   4. Damage to the non-dominant hemisphere (usually the right hemisphere) results in contralateral 【116†neglect syndrome】, inaccurate localization in the half field, impaired ability to judge distance (nondominant parietal lobe).
L215:   5. Large MCA infarcts often have 【117†déviation conjuguée】, a gaze preference towards the side of the lesion, especially during the acute period. Contralateral 【118†homonymous hemianopsia】 is often present.

L132: Basilar artery
L133: ---
L134: The basilar artery lies at the front of the 【66†brainstem】 in the midline and is formed from the union of the two 【67†vertebral arteries】.
L135: Diagram of the arterial circulation at the base of the brain (inferior view). The basilar artery terminates by splitting into the left and right 【68†posterior cerebral arteries】.

L152: 【83†Anatomical terminology】
L153: The basilar artery (U.K.: 【84†/ˈbæz.ɪ.lə/】;^{【85†[1]】}^{【86†[2]】} U.S.: 【84†/ˈbæs.ə.lər/】^{【87†[3]】}) is one of the 【88†arteries】 that supplies the 【89†brain】 with oxygen-rich blood.
L154: 
L155: The two 【67†vertebral arteries】 and the basilar artery are known as the vertebral basilar system, which supplies blood to the posterior part of the 【90†circle of Willis】 and joins with blood supplied to the anterior part of the circle of Willis from the 【91†internal carotid arteries】.^{【92†[4]】}^{【93†[5]】}^{【94†[6]】}
L156: ## Structure
L157: 
L158: [【95†edit】]
L159: 
L160: The diameter of the basilar artery range from 1.5 to 6.6 mm.^{【96†[7]】}
L161: 
L162: ### Origin
L163: 
L164: [【97†edit】]
L165: 
L166: The basilar artery arises from the union of the two 【67†vertebral arteries】 at the junction between the 【98†medulla oblongata】 and the 【73†pons】 between the 【99†abducens nerves】 (CN VI).^{【100†[8]】}
L167: ### Course
L168: 
L169: [【101†edit】]
L170: 
L171: It ascends along the 【102†basilar sulcus】 of the ventral 【73†pons】. It divides at the junction of the midbrain and pons into the 【68†posterior cerebral arteries】.
L172: 
L173: ### Branches
L174: 
L175: [【103†edit】]
L176: 
L177: Its branches from caudal to rostral include:
L178: 
L179:   * 【70†anterior inferior cerebellar artery】
L180:   * 【104†labyrinthine artery】 (<15% of people, usually branches from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery)
L181:   * 【69†pontine arteries】
L182:   * 【72†superior cerebellar artery】
L183: ## Clinical relevance
L184: 
L185: [【105†edit】]
L186: 
L187: A basilar artery stroke classically leads to 【106†locked-in syndrome】.^{【107†[9]】}^{【108†[10]】}

L198: ## References

L117: 【44†Anatomical terminology】
L118: The thalamogeniculate artery is either a single artery or group of smaller arteries^{【45†[1]】} arising from the 【38†posterior cerebral artery】 (distal to the origin of the 【46†posterior communicating artery】).^{【47†[2]】}^{【45†[1]】} It is part of the 【48†posterolateral central arteries】.^{【47†[2]】} It supplies parts of the 【49†thalamus】 (including the geniculate nuclei).^{【47†[2]】}^{【45†[1]】}
L119: ## Anatomy
L120: 
L121: [【50†edit】]
L122: 
L123: ### Distribution
L124: 
L125: [【51†edit】]
L126: 
L127: According to the 42th Edition of 【52†Gray's Anatomy】, the thalamogeniculate arteries supply the posterior thalamus, and 【53†medial geniculate nucleus】.^{【47†[2]】}
L128: 
L129: According to the Medical Dictionary of the French Academy of Medicine, it supplies the 【54†ventral lateral nucleus】 of thalamus, and the geniculate nuclei.^{【45†[1]】}
L130: ## Clinical significance
L131: 
L132: [【55†edit】]
L133: 
L134: A loss of supply of this artery presents clinically with sensory disturbances, and restlessness.^{【56†[3]】}

L123: Posterior communicating artery
L124: ---
L125: Schematic representation of the 【57†arterial circle】 and arteries of the brain (inferior view). Blood flows up to the brain through the vertebral arteries and the internal carotid arteries.
L126: The 【58†brain】 and the arteries of the base of the brain, viewed from below, with the front of the brain at the top of the image. The 【59†temporal】 pole of the 【60†cerebrum】 and a portion of the 【61†cerebellar】 hemisphere have been removed on the right side.
L127: Details
L128: ---
L129: Identifiers
L130: ---
L131: 【62†Latin】  | arteria cerebri communicans posterior
L132: 【63†TA98】  | 【64†A12.2.06.018†ifaa.unifr.ch】
L133: 【63†TA2】  | 【65†4521†ta2viewer.openanatomy.org】
L134: 【66†FMA】  | 【67†50084†bioportal.bioontology.org】
L135: 【68†Anatomical terminology】
L136: In 【69†human anatomy】, the left and right posterior communicating arteries are small^{【70†[1]】}^{: 471 } 【71†arteries】 at the base of the 【58†brain】 that form part of the 【57†circle of Willis】.
L137: 
L138: Anteriorly, it unites with the 【72†internal carotid artery】 (ICA) (prior to the terminal bifurcation of the ICA into the 【73†anterior cerebral artery】 and 【74†middle cerebral artery】); posteriorly, it unites with the 【75†posterior cerebral artery】.
L139: With the 【76†anterior communicating artery】, the posterior communicating arteries establish a system of 【77†collateral circulation】 in 【78†cerebral circulation】.
L140: ## Anatomy
L141: 
L142: [【79†edit】]
L143: 
L144: The arteries contribute to the blood supply of the 【80†optic tract】.^{【70†[1]】}^{: 465 }
L145: 
L146: The two posterior communicating arteries often differ in size.^{【70†[1]】}^{: 472 }
L147: ### Relations
L148: 
L149: [【81†edit】]
L150: 
L151: Each posterior communicating artery is situated within the 【82†interpeduncular cistern】, superolateral to the pituitary gland.^{【83†[2]】}^{: 450 } Each are is situated upon the medial surface of the ipsilateral 【84†cerebral peduncle】^{【70†[1]】}^{: 477 } and adjacent to the 【85†anterior perforated substance】.^{【70†[1]】}^{: 471 }
L152: The ipsilateral 【86†oculomotor nerve (CN III)】 passes inferolaterally to the artery^{【70†[1]】}^{: 494 } (pathology of the artery may thus compress the CN III^{【87†[3]】}^{: 407 }).
L153: ### Development
L154: 
L155: [【88†edit】]
L156: 
L157: The development of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) in the fetal brain occurs relatively late and arises from the fusion of several embryonic vessels near the caudal end of the posterior communicating artery.
L158: The PCA begins as a continuation of the posterior communicating artery in 70-90% of fetuses with the remainder of PCAs having a basilar origin. The fetal carotid origin of the PCA usually regresses as the vertebral and basilar arteries become dominant and it finds a new origin in the basilar artery. About 20% of adults retain PCA origin from the posterior communicating artery, and in turn, the internal carotid arteries.^{【89†[4]】}
L159: ## Function
L160: 
L161: [【90†edit】]
L162: 
L163: The brain is supplied with blood by the internal carotid arteries and also by the posterior cerebral arteries; the posterior communicating arteries connects the two systems. This provides redundancies or 【77†collaterals】 in the cerebral circulation so that, if one system is blocked or narrowed, the other can take over.
L164: ## Clinical significance
L165: 
L166: [【91†edit】]
L167: 
L168: 【92†Aneurysms】 of the posterior communicating artery are the third most common circle of Willis 【93†aneurysm】^{【94†[5]】} (the most common are 【76†anterior communicating artery】 aneurysms) and can lead to 【86†oculomotor nerve】 【95†palsy】.^{【96†[6]】}

L147: Internal carotid artery
L148: ---
L149: 【83†Carotid arteries】.
L150: Arteries of the neck. The internal carotid arteries arise from the 【84†common carotid arteries】 - labeled Common caroti on the figure.

L164: 【103†Anatomical terminology】
L165: The internal carotid artery is an 【104†artery】 in the 【105†neck】 which supplies the 【90†anterior】 and 【91†middle】 【106†cerebral circulation】.^{【107†[1]】}
L166: In human anatomy, the internal and 【108†external】 carotid arise from the 【84†common carotid artery】, where it bifurcates at 【109†cervical vertebrae】 C3 or C4. The internal carotid artery supplies the 【110†brain】, including the eyes,^{【111†[2]】} while the external carotid nourishes other portions of the head, such as the 【112†face】, 【113†scalp】, 【114†skull】, and 【115†meninges】.
L167: ## Classification
L168: 
L169: [【116†edit】]
L170: 
L171: 【98†Terminologia Anatomica】 in 1998 subdivided the artery into four parts: "cervical", "petrous", "cavernous", and "cerebral".^{【117†[3]】}^{【118†[4]】}
L172: In clinical settings, however, usually the classification system of the internal carotid artery follows the 1996 recommendations by Bouthillier,^{【119†[5]】} describing seven anatomical segments of the internal carotid artery, each with a corresponding alphanumeric identifier: C1 cervical; C2 petrous; C3 lacerum; C4 cavernous; C5 clinoid; C6 ophthalmic; and C7 communicating. The Bouthillier nomenclature remains in widespread use by neurosurgeons, neuroradiologists and neurologists.
L173: The segments are subdivided based on anatomical and microsurgical landmarks and surrounding anatomy, more than 【120†angiographic】 appearance of the artery. An alternative 【121†embryologic】 classification system proposed by 【122†Pierre Lasjaunias†fr.wikipedia.org】^{【123†[6]】} and colleagues is invaluable when it comes to explanation of many internal carotid artery variants. An older clinical classification, based on pioneering work by Fischer,^{【124†[7]】} is mainly of historical significance.
L174: Internal carotid artery
L175: 
L176: The segments of the internal carotid artery are as follows:
L177:   * Cervical segment, or C1, identical to the commonly used 【125†cervical portion】
L178:   * Petrous segment, or C2
L179:   * Lacerum segment, or C3
L180:     * C2 and C3 compose the commonly termed 【126†petrous portion】
L181:   * Cavernous segment, or C4, almost identical to the commonly used 【127†cavernous portion】
L182:   * Clinoid segment, or C5. This segment is not identified in some earlier classifications and lies between the commonly used 【127†cavernous portion】 and 【128†cerebral or supraclinoid portion】.
L183:   * Ophthalmic, or supraclinoid segment, or C6
L184:   * Communicating, or terminal segment, or C7
L185:     * C6 and C7 together constitute the commonly used 【128†cerebral or supraclinoid portion】.
L186: ## Course/part
L187: 
L188: [【129†edit】]
L189: 
L190: Segments of the internal carotid artery, delineated on an 【130†MRA】 of the head.
L191: 
L192: The internal carotid artery is a terminal branch of the 【84†common carotid artery】; it arises around the level of the fourth cervical 【131†vertebra】 when the common carotid bifurcates into this artery and its more superficial counterpart, the 【108†external carotid artery】.
L193: ### C1: Cervical segment
L194: 
L195: [【132†edit】]
L196: 
L197: Level of 6th cervical vertebrae - still at level of common carotid but relationships are similar to those of cervical segment of internal carotid
L198: 
L199: The cervical segment, or C1, or cervical part of the internal carotid, extends from the carotid bifurcation until it enters the 【133†carotid canal】 in the skull anterior to the 【134†jugular foramen】.
L200: 
L201: Internal carotid artery - dissection
L202: At its origin, the internal carotid artery is somewhat dilated. This part of the artery is known as the 【135†carotid sinus】 or the carotid bulb. The ascending portion of the cervical segment occurs distal to the bulb when the vessel walls are again parallel.
L203: The internal carotid runs vertically upward in the 【136†carotid sheath】 and enters the 【137†skull】 through the 【133†carotid canal】. During this part of its course, it lies in front of the 【138†transverse processes】 of the upper three cervical vertebrae.
L204: It is relatively superficial at its start, where it is contained in the 【139†carotid triangle】 of the neck, and lies behind and medial to the external carotid, overlapped by the 【140†sternocleidomastoid】 muscle, and covered by the deep fascia, the 【141†platysma】, and integument: it then passes beneath the 【142†parotid gland】, being crossed by the 【143†hypoglossal nerve】, the 【144†digastric muscle】 and the 【145†stylohyoid muscle】, the 【146†occipital artery】 and the 【147†posterior auricular artery】.
L205: Higher up, it is separated from the external carotid by the 【148†styloglossus】 and 【149†stylopharyngeus】 muscles, the tip of the 【150†styloid process】 and the 【151†stylohyoid ligament】, the 【152†glossopharyngeal nerve】 and the pharyngeal branch of the 【153†vagus nerve】.
L206: It is in relation, behind, with the 【154†longus capitis】, the 【155†superior cervical ganglion】 of the 【156†sympathetic trunk】, and the 【157†superior laryngeal nerve】; laterally, with the 【94†internal jugular vein】 and 【153†vagus nerve】, the nerve lying on a plane posterior to the artery; medially, with the 【158†pharynx】, 【157†superior laryngeal nerve】, and 【159†ascending pharyngeal artery】.
L207: At the base of the skull the 【152†glossopharyngeal】, vagus, 【160†accessory】, and 【143†hypoglossal】 nerves lie between the artery and the 【94†internal jugular vein】.
L208: Unlike the 【108†external carotid artery】, the internal carotid normally has no branches in the 【105†neck】.
L209: ### C2: Petrous segment
L210: 
L211: [【161†edit】]
L212: 
L213: The petrous segment, or C2, of the internal carotid, is that which is inside the petrous part of the 【162†temporal bone】. This segment extends until the 【163†foramen lacerum】.
L214: 
L215: The petrous portion classically has three sections:
L216: 
L217:   * an ascending, or vertical, portion;
L218:   * the genu, or bend; and
L219:   * the horizontal portion.
L220: When the internal carotid artery enters the canal in the 【164†petrous portion of the temporal bone】, it first ascends a short distance and then curves anteriorly and medially. The artery lies at first in front of the 【165†cochlea】 and 【166†tympanic cavity】; from the latter cavity it is separated by a thin, bony lamella, which is cribriform in the young subject, and often partly absorbed in old age.
L221: Farther forward, it is separated from the 【167†trigeminal ganglion】 by a thin plate of bone, which forms the floor of the fossa for the ganglion and the roof of the horizontal portion of the canal. Frequently this bony plate is more or less deficient, and then the ganglion is separated from the artery by fibrous membrane.
L222: The artery is separated from the bony wall of the 【133†carotid canal】 by a prolongation of 【168†dura mater】 and is surrounded by a number of small veins and by filaments of the 【169†carotid plexus】, derived from the ascending branch of the 【155†superior cervical ganglion】 of the sympathetic trunk.
L223: The named branches of the petrous segment of the internal carotid artery are:
L224: 
L225:   * the 【170†vidian artery】 or artery of the pterygoid canal
L226:   * the 【171†caroticotympanic artery】
L227: ### C3: Lacerum segment
L228: 
L229: [【172†edit】]
L230: The lacerum segment, or C3, is a short segment that begins above the 【163†foramen lacerum】 and ends at the 【173†petrolingual ligament】, a reflection of 【174†periosteum】 between the lingula and petrous apex (or petrosal process) of the 【175†sphenoid bone】. The lacerum portion is still considered "extradural" since it is surrounded by periosteum and fibrocartilage along its course. It is erroneously stated in several anatomy textbooks that the internal carotid artery passes through the foramen lacerum.
L231: This at best has only ever been a partial truth in that it passes through the superior part of the foramen on its way to the cavernous sinus. As such it does not traverse the skull through it. The inferior part of the foramen is actually filled with fibrocartilage. The broad consensus is that the internal carotid artery should not be described as travelling through the foramen lacerum.^{【176†[8]】}
L232: ### C4: Cavernous segment
L233: 
L234: [【177†edit】]
L235: 
L236: Oblique section through the cavernous sinus.

L122: ---

L136: 【64†Anatomical terminology】
L137: The superior cerebellar artery (SCA) is an 【65†artery】 of the head. It arises near the end of the 【54†basilar artery】. It is a branch of the basilar artery. It supplies parts of the 【57†cerebellum】, the 【66†midbrain】, and other nearby structures. It is the cause of 【67†trigeminal neuralgia】 in some patients.
L138: ## Structure
L139: 
L140: [【68†edit】]
L141: The superior cerebellar artery arises near the end of the 【54†basilar artery】.^{【69†[1]】} It passes laterally around the brainstem.^{【69†[1]】} This is immediately below the 【70†oculomotor nerve】,^{【69†[1]】} which separates it from the 【71†posterior cerebral artery】. It then winds around the 【72†cerebral peduncle】, close to the 【73†trochlear nerve】.
L142: It also lies close to the 【74†cerebellar tentorium】.^{【69†[1]】} When it arrives at the upper surface of the 【57†cerebellum】, it divides into branches which ramify in the 【75†pia mater】 and anastomose with those of the 【76†anterior inferior cerebellar arteries】 and the 【77†posterior inferior cerebellar arteries】.
L143: Several branches are given to the 【78†pineal body】, the 【79†anterior medullary velum】, and the 【80†tela chorioidea】 of the 【81†third ventricle】.
L144: ## Function
L145: 
L146: [【82†edit】]
L147: 
L148: The arteries of the base of the brain. Superior cerebellar artery labeled near center. The 【83†temporal】 pole of the 【84†cerebrum】 and a portion of the 【57†cerebellar】 hemisphere have been removed on the right side (left half of diagram). Inferior aspect (viewed from below).
L149: The superior cerebellar artery supplies deep parts and superior parts of the 【57†cerebellum】.^{【69†[1]】}^{【85†[2]】} It supplies parts of the 【66†midbrain】 (tectum, including the 【86†cerebral crus】).^{【69†[1]】} It also supplies 【87†superior medullary velum】, the 【88†superior cerebellar peduncle】, the 【89†middle cerebellar peduncle】, and the interpeduncular region.^{【69†[1]】}
L150: ## Clinical significance
L151: 
L152: [【90†edit】]
L153: 
L154: ### Trigeminal neuralgia
L155: 
L156: [【91†edit】]
L157: 
L158: The superior cerebellar artery frequently causes 【67†trigeminal neuralgia】 by compressing the 【92†trigeminal nerve】 (CN V) causing 【93†facial pain】 (the distribution of the nerve). Vascular 【94†microsurgery】 may be able to decompress the trigeminal nerve.^{【85†[2]】} At autopsy, 50% of people without trigeminal neuralgia will also be noted to have vascular compression of the nerve.^{【95†[3]】}
L159: ### Stroke
L160: 
L161: [【96†edit】]
L162: 
L163: An 【97†infarction】 of the superior cerebellar artery can cause a 【98†cerebellar stroke】.^{【99†[4]】} This can cause a 【100†headache】 and 【101†ataxia】 (with problems walking).^{【99†[4]】}

L161: 【94†Anatomical terminology】
L162: The ophthalmic artery (OA) is an artery of the head. It is the first branch of the 【69†internal carotid artery】 distal to the 【95†cavernous sinus】. Branches of the ophthalmic artery supply all the structures in the 【96†orbit】 around the 【97†eye】, as well as some structures in the 【98†nose】, 【99†face】, and 【100†meninges】. Occlusion of the ophthalmic artery or its branches can produce sight-threatening conditions.
L163: ## Structure
L164: 
L165: [【101†edit】]
L166: The ophthalmic artery emerges from the 【69†internal carotid artery】.^{【102†[1]】} This is usually just after the internal carotid artery emerges from the cavernous sinus. In some cases, the ophthalmic artery branches just before the internal carotid exits the carotid sinus. The ophthalmic artery emerges along the medial side of the 【103†anterior clinoid process】.
L167: It runs anteriorly, passing through the 【104†optic canal】 inferolaterally to the 【105†optic nerve】.^{【102†[1]】} It can also pass superiorly to the optic nerve in a minority of cases.^{【106†[2]】} In the posterior third of the cone of the orbit, the ophthalmic artery turns sharply and medially to run along the medial wall of the orbit.
L168: Because of the obvious importance of the ocular globe, branches of the ophthalmic artery often are subdivided into two groups: those that supply the eyeball (ocular group) and those that supply non-ocular orbital structures (orbital group).^{【107†[3]】}
L169: ### Orbital group
L170: 
L171: [【108†edit】]
L172: 
L173: The orbital group, distributing vessels to the orbit and surrounding parts, includes:
L174:   * 【70†Lacrimal artery】 A. lacrimalis;
L175:   * 【71†Supraorbital artery】 A. supraorbitalis;
L176:   * 【72†Posterior ethmoidal artery】 A. ethmoidalis posterior;
L177:   * 【73†Anterior ethmoidal artery】 A. ethmoidalis anterior;
L178:   * 【109†Medial palpebral artery】 A. palpebralis medialis;
L179:   * 【110†Frontal artery】, also called the 【75†Supratrochlear artery】 A. supratrochlearis;
L180:   * 【76†Dorsal nasal artery】 A. dorsalis nasi.
L181: ### Ocular group
L182: 
L183: [【111†edit】]
L184: 
L185: The ocular group, distributing vessels to the eye and its muscles, includes:
L186: 
L187:   * 【77†Long posterior ciliary arteries】 Aa. ciliares posteriores longae;
L188:   * 【78†Short posterior ciliary arteries】 Aa. ciliares posteriores breves;
L189:   * 【79†Anterior ciliary artery】 A. ciliares anterior;
L190:   * 【80†Central retinal artery】 A. centralis retinae.
L191: ### Central retinal artery
L192: 
L193: [【112†edit】]
L194: 
L195: The 【113†central retinal artery】 is the first, and one of the smaller branches of the ophthalmic artery and runs in the dura mater inferior to the optic nerve. About 12.5mm (0.5 inch) posterior to the globe, the central retinal artery turns superiorly and penetrates the 【105†optic nerve】, continuing along the center of the optic nerve, entering the eye to supply the inner retinal layers.
L196: ### Lacrimal artery
L197: 
L198: [【114†edit】]
L199: 
L200: The next branch of the ophthalmic artery is the 【70†lacrimal artery】, one of the largest, arises just as the OA enters the orbit and runs along the superior edge of the 【115†lateral rectus muscle】 to supply the 【116†lacrimal gland】, 【117†eyelids】 and 【118†conjunctiva】.
L201: ### Posterior ciliary arteries
L202: 
L203: [【119†edit】]
L204: The ophthalmic artery then turns medially, giving off 1 to 5 【120†posterior ciliary arteries】 (PCA) that subsequently branch into the long and short posterior ciliary arteries (LPCA and SPCA respectively) which perforate the sclera posteriorly in the vicinity of the optic nerve and macula to supply the posterior uveal tract. In the past, anatomists made little distinction between the posterior ciliary arteries and the short and long posterior ciliary arteries often using the terms synonymously.
L205: However, recent work by Hayreh has shown that there is both an anatomic and clinically useful distinction.^{【121†[4]】} The PCAs arise directly from the OA and are end arteries which is to say no PCA or any of its branches anastomose with any other artery. Consequently, sudden occlusion of any PCA will produce an infarct in the region of the choroid supplied by that particular PCA.
L206: Occlusion of a short or long PCA will produce a smaller choroidal infarct, within the larger area supplied by the specific parent PCA.
L207: ### Muscular branches
L208: 
L209: [【122†edit】]
L210: 
L211: The ophthalmic artery continues medially the superior and inferior muscular branches arise either from the ophthalmic artery directly or a single trunk from the ophthalmic artery subsequently divides into superior and inferior branches to supply the 【123†extraocular muscles】.
L212: ### Supraorbital artery
L213: 
L214: [【124†edit】]
L215: 
L216: The 【71†supraorbital artery】 branches from the ophthalmic artery as it passes over the optic nerve. The supraorbital artery passes anteriorly along the medial border of the 【125†superior rectus】 and 【126†levator palpebrae】 and through the 【127†supraorbital foramen】 to supply muscles and skin of the forehead.
L217: ### Ethmoidal arteries
L218: 
L219: [【128†edit】]
L220: 
L221: After reaching the medial wall of the orbit, the ophthalmic artery again turns anteriorly. The 【72†posterior ethmoidal artery】 enters the nose via the posterior ethmoidal canal and supplies the posterior ethmoidal sinuses and enters the skull to supply the meninges.
L222: The OA continues anteriorly, giving off the 【73†anterior ethmoidal artery】 which enters the nose after traversing the anterior ethmoidal canal and supplies the anterior and middle ethmoidal sinuses, as well as the frontal sinus and also enters the cranium to supply the meninges.
L223: ### Medial palpebral arteries
L224: 
L225: [【129†edit】]
L226: 
L227: The OA continues anteriorly to the trochlea, where the medial palpebral arteries (superior and inferior) arise and supply the eyelids.
L228: 
L229: ### Terminal branches
L230: 
L231: [【130†edit】]
L232: 
L233: The OA terminates in two branches, the supratrochlear (or frontal) artery and the dorsal nasal artery. Both exit the orbit medially to supply the forehead and scalp.
L234: ## Function
L235: 
L236: [【131†edit】]
L237: 
L238: Branches of the ophthalmic artery supply:
L239: 
L240:   * 【132†Frontal belly】 of the 【133†occipitofrontalis muscle】
L241:   * 【134†Inferior oblique muscle】
L242:   * 【135†Inferior rectus muscle】
L243:   * 【116†Lacrimal gland】
L244:   * 【115†Lateral rectus muscle】
L245:   * 【126†Levator palpebrae superioris muscle】
L246:   * 【136†Medial rectus muscle】
L247:   * 【137†Nasalis muscle】
L248:   * 【138†Procerus muscle】
L249:   * 【139†Superior oblique muscle】
L250:   * 【125†Superior rectus muscle】
L251: ## Clinical significance
L252: 
L253: [【140†edit】]
L254: 
L255: Further information: 【141†Ocular ischemic syndrome】
L256: Severe occlusion of the ophthalmic artery causes 【141†ocular ischemic syndrome】. As with 【113†central retinal artery】 occlusions, ophthalmic artery occlusions may result from systemic 【142†cardiovascular diseases】; however, a 【143†cherry-red spot】 is typically absent and the vision is usually worse.
L257: 【144†Amaurosis fugax】 is a temporary loss of vision that occurs in two conditions which cause a temporary reduction in ophthalmic artery pressure: 【145†orthostatic hypotension】 and positive acceleration.^{【146†[5]】}
L258: Even complete occlusion of the ophthalmic artery may possibly leave the eye without symptoms, probably because of 【147†circulatory anastomoses】^{【148†[6]】}

L119: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
L120: ---
L121: The three major arteries of the cerebellum: the 【53†SCA】, 【54†AICA】, and PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar artery)
L122: Diagram of the arterial circulation at the base of the brain (inferior view). PICA is labeled at bottom right.
L123: Details
L124: ---
L125: Source  | 【55†Vertebral artery】
L126: Branches  | Medial branch
L127: lateral
L128: 【56†Vein】  | 【57†Inferior cerebellar veins】
L129: Supplies  | 【58†Cerebellum】, 【59†choroid plexus】 of the 【60†fourth ventricle】
L130: Identifiers
L131: ---
L132: 【61†Latin】  | arteria inferior posterior cerebelli
L133: 【62†TA98】  | 【63†A12.2.08.012†ifaa.unifr.ch】
L134: 【62†TA2】  | 【64†4542†ta2viewer.openanatomy.org】
L135: 【65†FMA】  | 【66†50518†bioportal.bioontology.org】
L136: 【67†Anatomical terminology】
L137: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) is the largest branch of the 【55†vertebral artery】. It is one of the three main 【68†arteries】 that supply blood to the 【58†cerebellum】, a part of the 【69†brain】. Blockage of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery can result in a type of 【70†stroke】 called 【71†lateral medullary syndrome】.
L138: ## Supply
L139: 
L140: [【72†edit】]
L141: 
L142: The PICA supplies blood to the 【73†medulla oblongata】; the 【59†choroid plexus】 and 【74†tela choroidea】 of the 【60†fourth ventricle】; the 【75†cerebellar tonsils】; the 【76†inferior vermis】, and the inferior parts of the 【58†cerebellum】.^{【77†[1]】}
L143: ### Course
L144: 
L145: [【78†edit】]
L146: 
L147: It winds backward around the upper part of the 【73†medulla oblongata】, passing between the origins of the 【79†vagus nerve】 and the 【80†accessory nerve】, over the 【81†inferior cerebellar peduncle】 to the undersurface of the 【58†cerebellum】, where it divides into two branches.
L148: The medial branch continues backward to the notch between the two hemispheres of the cerebellum; while the lateral supplies the under surface of the cerebellum, as far as its lateral border, where it 【82†anastomoses】 with the 【54†anterior inferior cerebellar】 and the 【53†superior cerebellar】 branches of the 【83†basilar artery】.
L149: 
L150: Branches from this artery supply the 【59†choroid plexus】 of the 【60†fourth ventricle】.
L151: ## Clinical significance
L152: 
L153: [【84†edit】]
L154: 
L155: A disrupted blood supply to posterior inferior cerebellar artery due to a 【85†thrombus】 or 【86†embolus】 can result in a 【70†stroke】 and lead to 【71†lateral medullary syndrome】. Severe occlusion of this artery or to vertebral arteries could lead to 【87†Horner's Syndrome】 as well.

L146: 【81†Anatomical terminology】
L147: The posterior cerebral artery (PCA) is one of a pair of 【82†cerebral arteries】 that supply oxygenated 【83†blood】 to the 【70†occipital lobe】, as well as the medial and inferior aspects of the 【71†temporal lobe】 of the 【84†human brain】. The two 【85†arteries】 originate from the distal end of the 【67†basilar artery】, where it bifurcates into the left and right posterior cerebral arteries.
L148: These anastomose with the 【86†middle cerebral arteries】 and 【87†internal carotid arteries】 via the 【88†posterior communicating arteries】.
L149: ## Structure
L150: 
L151: [【89†edit】]
L152: 
L153: The posterior cerebral artery is subdivided into 4 segments:
L154: 
L155: P1: pre-communicating segment
L156: 
L157:   * Originated at the termination of the basilar artery
L158:   * May give rise to the artery of Percheron if present
L159: 
L160: P2: post-communicating segment
L161: 
L162:   * From the PCOM around the midbrain
L163:   * Terminates as it enters the quadrigeminal ganglion
L164:   * Gives rise to the choroidal branches (medial and lateral posterior choroidal arteries)
L165: 
L166: P3: quadrigeminal segment
L167:   * Courses posteromedially through the quadrigeminal cistern
L168:   * Terminates as it enters the sulk of the occipital lobe
L169: 
L170: P4: cortical segment
L171: 
L172:   * Within the sulci of the occipital lobe
L173: 
L174: The branches of the posterior cerebral artery are divided into two sets, ganglionic and cortical.
L175: ### Central branches
L176: 
L177: [【90†edit】]
L178: 
L179: See also: 【91†Artery of Percheron】
L180: 
L181: The following are central branches of the PCA, also known as perforating branches:
L182:   * Thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate or postero-medial ganglionic branches: a group of small arteries which arise at the commencement of the posterior cerebral artery: these, with similar branches from the 【92†posterior communicating】, pierce the posterior perforated substance, and supply the medial surfaces of the 【93†thalami】 and the walls of the 【94†third ventricle】.
L183:   * Peduncular perforating or postero-lateral ganglionic branches: small arteries which arise from the posterior cerebral artery after it has turned around the 【95†cerebral peduncle】; they supply a considerable portion of the thalamus.
L184: Posterior cerebral artery
L185: ### Posterior (choroidal) branches
L186: 
L187: [【96†edit】]
L188: 
L189: The posterior choroidal branches of the posterior cerebral artery are sometimes referred to as a single posterior choroidal artery.
L190:   * Medial posterior choroidal branches: run forward beneath the 【97†splenium】 of the 【98†corpus callosum】, and supply the 【99†tela choroidea of the third ventricle】 and the 【100†choroid plexus】.
L191:   * Lateral posterior choroidal branches: small branches to the cerebral peduncle, fornix, thalamus, caudate nucleus, and choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle.^{【101†[1]】}
L192: ### Cortical branches
L193: 
L194: [【102†edit】]
L195: 
L196: The cortical branches are:
L197:   * Anterior temporal, distributed to the 【103†uncus】 and the anterior part of the 【104†fusiform gyrus】
L198:   * Posterior temporal, to the fusiform and the 【105†inferior temporal gyri】
L199:   * Lateral occipital, which branches into the anterior, middle and posterior inferior temporal arteries
L200:   * Medial occipital, which branches into the:
L201:     * 【106†Calcarine sulcus】, to the 【107†cuneus】 and 【108†lingual gyrus】 and the back part of the convex surface of the 【70†occipital lobe】
L202:     * 【109†Parieto-occipital sulcus】, to the 【107†cuneus】 and the 【110†precuneus】
L203:   * Splenial, or the posterior pericallosal branch, sometimes 【111†anastomoses】 with the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), and may not be present if the ACA wraps around the corpus callosum
L204: ## Development
L205: 
L206: [【112†edit】]
L207: 
L208: The 【113†prenatal development】 of the posterior cerebral arteries in the 【114†fetus】 comes relatively late and arises from the fusion of several embryonic vessels near the caudal ends of the 【88†posterior communicating arteries】 supplying the 【115†mesencephalon】 and 【116†diencephalon】.^{【117†[2]】} The PCA thus begins as a continuation of the PCommA in the fetus with only 10–30% of fetuses showing a prominent 【67†basilar】 origin.^{【118†[3]】}
L209: The fetal carotid origin of the PCA usually regresses as the vertebral and basilar arteries develop with the posterior communicating artery reducing in size. In most adults, the PCA sources from the anterior portion of the basilar artery. About 19% of adults retain PCommA dominance of the PCA, with 72% having dominant basilar origin, and the rest having either equal prominence between PCommA and basilar artery, or a single exclusive source.^{【118†[3]】}
L210: ## Clinical significance
L211: 
L212: [【119†edit】]
L213: ### Stroke
L214: 
L215: [【120†edit】]
L216: 
L217: See also: 【121†Posterior cerebral artery syndrome】
L218:   * Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensations.
L219:   * Visual field defects (contralateral 【122†hemianopsia】 with macular sparing).^{【123†[4]】}
L220:   * 【124†Prosopagnosia】 with bilateral obstruction of the lingual and fusiform gyri.
L221:   * Superior Alternating Syndrome (【125†Weber's syndrome】)^{【126†[5]】}
L222:   * Ipsilateral deficits of 【127†oculomotor nerve】.
L223:   * Contralateral deficits of 【128†facial nerve】 (only lower face, upper face receives bilateral input), 【129†vagus nerve】 and 【130†hypoglossal nerve】.
L224:   * 【131†Horner's Syndrome】^{【132†[6]】}
L225: Signs and symptoms: Structures involved
L226: ### Peripheral territory (cortical branches)
L227: 
L228: [【133†edit】]
L229:   * Homonymous 【122†hemianopsia】 (often upper quadrantic): Calcarine cortex or optic radiation nearby.^{【123†[4]】}
L230:   * Bilateral homonymous hemianopsia, cortical blindness, awareness or denial of blindness; tactile naming, achromatopia (color blindness), failure to see to-and-fro movements, inability to perceive objects not centrally located, apraxia of ocular movements, inability to count or enumerate objects, tendency to run into things that the patient sees and tries to avoid: Bilateral occipital lobe with possibly the parietal lobe involved.
L231:   * Verbal dyslexia without agraphia, color anomia: Dominant calcarine lesion and posterior part of corpus callosum.^{【123†[4]】}
L232:   * Memory defect: Hippocampal lesion bilaterally or on the dominant side only.^{【123†[4]】}
L233:   * Topographic disorientation and prosopagnosia: Usually with lesions of nondominant, calcarine, and lingual gyrus.
L234:   * Simultanagnosia, hemivisual neglect: Dominant visual cortex, contralateral hemisphere.
L235:   * Unformed visual hallucinations, peduncular hallucinosis, metamorphopsia, teleopsia, illusory visual spread, palinopsia, distortion of outlines, central photophobia: Calcarine cortex.^{【123†[4]】}
L236:   * Complex hallucinations: Usually nondominant hemisphere.^{【123†[4]】}
L237: ### Central territory (ganglionic branches)
L238: 
L239: [【134†edit】]
L240:   * Thalamic syndrome: sensory loss (all modalities), spontaneous pain and dysesthesias, choreoathetosis, intention tremor, spasms of hand, mild hemiparesis, contralateral hemianaethesia: Posteroventral nucleus of thalamus; involvement of the adjacent subthalamus body or its afferent tracts.
L241:   * Thalamoperforate syndrome: crossed cerebellar ataxia with ipsilateral third nerve palsy (Claude's syndrome): Dentatothalamic tract and issuing third nerve.^{【135†[7]】}
L242:   * Weber's syndrome: third nerve palsy and contralateral hemiplegia: Third nerve and cerebral peduncle.^{【126†[5]】}
L243:   * Contralateral hemiplegia: Cerebral peduncle.
L244:   * Paralysis or paresis of vertical eye movement, skew deviation, sluggish pupillary responses to light, slight miosis and ptosis (retraction nystagmus and "tucking" of the eyelids may be associated): Supranuclear fibers to third nerve, interstitial nucleus of Cajal, nucleus of Darkschewitsch, and posterior commissure.
L245:   * Contralateral rhythmic, ataxic action tremor; rhythmic postural or "holding" tremor (rubral tremor): Dentatothalamic tract.

L114: This article is about arteries at the base of the brain. For another artery, see 【48†Central retinal artery】. For the Boston highway, see 【49†Central Artery】.
L115: 
L116: Central arteries
L117: ---
L118: Details
L119: ---
L120: Source  | 【50†Circle of Willis】
L121: 【51†Anatomical terminology】
L122: Central arteries (or perforating or ganglionic arteries) of the 【52†brain】 are numerous small 【53†arteries】 branching from the 【50†Circle of Willis】, and adjacent arteries that often enter the substance of the brain through the 【54†anterior】 and 【55†posterior perforated substances】. They supply structures of the base of the brain and internal structures of the cerebral hemispheres.
L123: They are separated into four principal groups: anteromedial central arteries; anterolateral central arteries (lenticulostriate arteries); posteromedial central arteries (paramedian arteries); and posterolateral central arteries.
L124: ## Anteromedial central arteries
L125: 
L126: [【56†edit】]
L127: Anteromedial central arteries^{【57†[1]】} (also anteromedial perforating arteries, or anteromedial ganglionic arteries) are arteries that arise from the 【58†anterior cerebral artery】 and 【59†anterior communicating artery】, and pass into the substance of the cerebral hemispheres through the (medial portion of) the 【54†anterior perforated substance】 to supply the 【60†optic chiasm】, (【61†anterior nucleus】, 【62†preoptic area】, and 【63†supraoptic nucleus】 of the) 【64†hypothalamus】, 【65†lamina terminalis】, 【66†septum pellucidum】, (anterior portions of the) 【67†columns of fornix】, 【68†rostrum of corpus callosum】, (anterior portion of) 【69†putamen】, head of 【70†caudate nucleus】, and 【71†cingulate cortex】.^{【72†[2]】}
L128: ## Anterolateral central arteries
L129: 
L130: [【73†edit】]
L131: The anterolateral central arteries or lenticulostriate arteries^{【74†[3]】} (also anterolateral perforating arteries, anterolateral ganglionic arteries, striate arteries, or lateral striate arteries; latin aa. centrales anterolaterales,^{【75†[4]】} or aa.
L132: lenticulostriatae^{【75†[4]】}) are a group of small arteries mostly arising from (the initial 【76†M1 part】 of) the 【77†middle cerebral artery】 that enter the brain through the 【54†anterior perforated substance】 to provide arterial supply to parts of the 【78†basal ganglia】.^{【72†[2]】} They are 【79†end arteries】.
L133: The name of these arteries is derived from some of the structures they supply, namely the 【80†lentiform nucleus】 and the 【81†striatum】.
L134: ### Distribution
L135: 
L136: [【82†edit】]
L137: 
L138: The ALCAs supply the:^{【83†[5]】}^{【72†[2]】}
L139: 
L140:   * posterior portion of the 【81†striatum】
L141:     * 【69†putamen】
L142:     * (head of) 【70†caudate nucleus】
L143:   * (lateral portion of) 【84†globus pallidus】
L144:   * (all parts of) 【85†internal capsule】 (【86†anterior limb】, 【87†genu】, and - a portion of - 【88†posterior limb】)
L145:   * 【89†claustrum】
L146:   * 【90†external capsule】
L147: The 【91†distal medial striate artery (Recurrent artery of Heubner)】 arises either from the middle cerebral artery or 【58†anterior cerebral artery】, and supplies the rostral/anterior portion of the caudate nucleus and putamen, and the anterior limb and genu of the 【85†internal capsule】.^{【72†[2]】}
L148: ### Clinical significance
L149: 
L150: [【92†edit】]
L151: 
L152: Blockage of the lenticulostriate arteries causes 【93†lacunar strokes】. These infarcts are most often due to 【94†hyaline arteriosclerosis】 secondary to 【95†hypertension】. This can lead to contralateral 【96†paresis】 (muscular weakness) and/or sensory loss of the face and body.
L153: ## Posteromedial central arteries
L154: 
L155: [【97†edit】]
L156: 
L157: The posteromedial central arteries or paramedian arteries^{【98†[6]】} (also posteromedial perforating arteries, or posteromedial ganglionic arteries^{【72†[2]】}) are branches of the 【99†posterior cerebral artery】, and 【100†posterior communicating artery】. They enter the substance of the brain through the 【55†posterior perforated substance】. They supply a large portion of the 【101†diencephalon】 as well as some subcortical 【102†telencephalic】 structures.
L158: The thalamoperforating arteries^{【103†[7]】} are posteromedial central arteries which supply parts of the 【104†thalamus】.^{【72†[2]】}^{【105†[8]】}^{【75†[4]】} According to the Medical Dictionary of the French Academy of Medicine, a single thalamoperforating artery arises from the (pre-communicating (P1) segment of) the 【99†posterior cerebral artery】, piercing the 【54†anterior perforated substance】 to reach and supply the ventral portion of the thalamus.^{【105†[8]】} The Sobotta Anatomy Textbook (2018) distinguishes an anterior thalamoperforating artery which arises from the 【100†posterior communicating artery】 and supplies the rostral portion of the thalamus, and a posterior thalamoperforating artery which supplies multiple 【106†thalamic nuclei】.^{【75†[4]】}
L159: ### Origin
L160: 
L161: [【107†edit】]
L162: PMCAs arise from the proximal (【108†pre-communicating segment】 (P1)^{【109†[9]】} of the 【99†posterior cerebral artery (PCA)】,^{【72†[2]】}^{【75†[4]】}^{【109†[9]】} and along the entire length of^{【72†[2]】} the 【100†posterior communicating artery】^{【72†[2]】}^{【110†[10]】}^{【83†[5]】}^{: 372 } (though branches arising from the latter may be considered as a distinct anatomical entity^{【75†[4]】}).
L163: The PMCAs thus arise at and near the bifurcation of the 【111†basilar artery】.^{【83†[5]】}^{: 378 } The PMCAs are the very first branches of the PCA.^{【83†[5]】}^{: 377 }
L164: ### Course
L165: 
L166: [【112†edit】]
L167: 
L168: PMCAs intermingle to form an extensive 【113†venous plexus】 in the 【114†interpeduncular fossa】^{【115†[11]】} before entering the substance of the brain through the 【55†posterior perforated substance】,^{【75†[4]】}^{【115†[11]】}^{【109†[9]】} then also passing through the posterior part of the 【85†internal capsule】 along their path.^{【116†[12]】}
L169: ### Distribution
L170: 
L171: [【117†edit】]
L172: 
L173: The PMCAs supply a substantial part of the diencephalon.^{【75†[4]】}
L174: 
L175: The PMCAs are distributed to:^{【72†[2]】}^{【75†[4]】}^{【83†[5]】}^{: 380 }
L176:   * 【84†globus pallidus】
L177:   * (lateral wall of) 【118†third ventricle】,
L178:   * (parts of the) 【104†thalamus】 (partially via the 【119†thalamoperforating artery】)^{【110†[10]】}
L179:   * 【120†subthalamus】
L180:   * 【64†hypothalamus】^{【109†[9]】}
L181:   * 【121†mammillary bodies】^{【109†[9]】}^{【110†[10]】}
L182:   * 【122†pituitary gland】
L183:   * 【60†optic chiasm】^{【110†[10]】} and 【123†tracts】^{【110†[10]】}
L184:   * 【124†tuber cinereum】^{【110†[10]】}
L185:   * 【125†posterior limb of internal capsule】^{【109†[9]】}
L186:   * 【126†mesencephalon (midbrain)】^{【83†[5]】}^{: 380 }
L187:     * 【127†basis pedunculi】
L188:     * 【128†substantia nigra】
L189:     * 【129†mesencephalic tegmentum】
L190: ### Clinical significance
L191: 
L192: [【130†edit】]
L193: An 【131†embolus】 passing along a vertebral artery will typically continue into the basilar artery before finally lodging at the bifurcation of the basilar artery, thus bilaterally obstructing the PMCAs (as well as the 【132†superior cerebellar artery】); such occlusion of the PMCAs will swiftly result in infarction of the 【133†reticular formation】 at the level of the mesencephalon-pons junction (resulting in coma) as well as destruction of the fibers of both 【134†oculomotor nerve (CN III)】 (resulting in divergence of both eyes, and fixed 【135†mydriasis】).^{【83†[5]】}^{: 377-378 }
L194: An embolism of a single PMCA at mesencephalic levels may result in a small infarction of the mesencephalon, causing 【136†Weber's syndrome】.^{【83†[5]】}^{: 378 }
L195: 
L196: 【137†Uncal herniation】 can cause compression of the PMCAs, which may result in 【138†Duret haemorrhages】.
L197: ## Posterolateral central arteries
L198: 
L199: [【139†edit】]
L200: 
L201: Posterolateral central arteries^{【140†[13]】} (also posterolateral perforating arteries, or posterolateral ganglionic arteries) are arteries that arise from the 【99†posterior cerebral artery】 distal to its first - pre-communicating (P1) -segment (i.e. distal to the origin of the 【100†posterior communicating artery】).^{【72†[2]】}
L202: 
L203: They are distributed to the:^{【83†[5]】}^{【72†[2]】}
L204:   * (lateral part of) 【141†cerebral peduncle】
L205:   * 【142†tectum】
L206:   * 【143†corpora quadrigemina】 (i.e. 【144†superior】 and 【145†inferior colliculi】)
L207:   * 【146†pineal gland】
L208:   * (via the 【147†thalamogeniculate arteries】) (the posterior parts of) 【104†thalamus】^{【148†[14]】}
L209:     * 【149†medial geniculate nucleus】
L210:     * 【150†lateral geniculate nucleus】
L211:     * 【151†ventral lateral nucleus of thalamus】

L213:

L138: Vertebral artery
L139: ---
L140: Arteries of the neck. The vertebral arteries arise from the subclavian arteries and join to form the 【72†basilar artery】
L141: Details
L142: ---
L143: Source  | 【73†Subclavian artery】
L144: Branches  | 【72†Basilar artery】
L145: 【74†Posterior spinal artery】
L146: 【75†Anterior spinal artery】
L147: 【76†Posterior inferior cerebellar artery】
L148: 【77†Vein】  | 【78†Vertebral vein】
L149: Identifiers
L150: ---
L151: 【79†Latin】  | arteria vertebralis
L152: 【80†MeSH】  | 【81†D014711†meshb.nlm.nih.gov】
L153: 【82†TA98】  | 【83†A12.2.08.002†ifaa.unifr.ch】
L154: 【82†TA2】  | 【84†4538†ta2viewer.openanatomy.org】
L155: 【85†FMA】  | 【86†3956†bioportal.bioontology.org】
L156: 【87†Anatomical terminology】
L157: The vertebral arteries are major 【88†arteries】 of the neck. Typically, the vertebral arteries originate from the 【89†subclavian arteries】. Each vessel courses superiorly along each side of the neck, merging within the skull to form the single, midline 【72†basilar artery】. As the supplying component of the vertebrobasilar vascular system, the vertebral arteries supply blood to the upper 【90†spinal cord】, 【91†brainstem】, 【92†cerebellum】, and 【93†posterior part of brain】.^{【94†[1]】}
L158: ## Structure
L159: 
L160: [【95†edit】]
L161: The vertebral artery typically arises from the superior aspect of the central subclavian artery on each side of the body,^{【96†[2]】} then enters deep to the transverse process at the level of the 6th 【97†cervical vertebrae】 (C6),^{【94†[1]】}.
L162: It then proceeds superiorly, in the 【98†transverse foramen】 of each 【99†cervical vertebra】.^{【94†[1]】} Once it has passed through the transverse foramen of C1 (also known as the 【100†atlas】), the vertebral artery travels across the posterior arch of C1 and through the 【101†suboccipital triangle】^{【102†[3]】} before entering the 【103†foramen magnum】.^{【94†[1]】}
L163: 【104†Nunziante Ippolito】, a Neapolitan physician, identified the "angle of Nunziante Ippolito" to find the vertebral artery, between the 【105†anterior scalene muscle】 and the 【106†longus colli】 muscle.^{【107†[4]】}
L164: Inside the skull, both vertebral arteries join to form the 【72†basilar artery】 at the base of the 【108†pons】. The 【72†basilar artery】 is the main blood supply to the 【91†brainstem】 and connects to the 【109†Circle of Willis】 to potentially supply the rest of the brain if there is compromise to one of the 【110†carotids】. At each cervical level, the vertebral artery sends branches to the surrounding musculature via the 【111†anterior spinal arteries】.
L165: 
L166: Segments of vertebral artery anterior projection
L167: The vertebral artery may be divided into four parts:
L168:   * The first (preforaminal) part runs upward and backward between the 【112†anterior scalene】 and the 【113†longus colli muscles】 (angle of Nunziante Ippolito). In front of it are the 【114†internal jugular】 and 【78†vertebral veins】, and is crossed by the 【115†inferior thyroid artery】; the left vertebral is also crossed by the 【116†thoracic duct】. Behind it are the transverse process of the seventh 【99†cervical vertebra】, the 【117†sympathetic trunk】 and its 【118†inferior cervical ganglion】
L169:   * The second (foraminal) part runs upward through the transverse foramina of the C6 to C2 vertebrae, and is surrounded by branches from the inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion and by a plexus of veins which unite to form the vertebral vein at the lower part of the neck. It is situated in front of the trunks of the cervical nerves, and pursues an almost vertical course as far as the 【119†transverse process of the axis】.
L170:   * The third (extradural or atlantic) part issues from the C2 foramen transversarium on the medial side of the 【120†Rectus capitis lateralis】.
L171: It is further subdivided into the vertical part V3v passing vertically upwards, crossing the C2 root and entering the foramen transversarium of C1, and the horizontal part V3h, curving medially and posteriorly behind the 【121†superior articular process of the atlas】, the anterior ramus of the first cervical nerve being on its medial side; it then lies in the groove on the upper surface of the posterior arch of the atlas, and enters the vertebral canal by passing beneath the 【122†posterior atlantoöccipital membrane】.
L172: This part of the artery is covered by the 【123†Semispinalis capitis】 and is contained in the 【101†suboccipital triangle】—a triangular space bounded by the 【124†Rectus capitis posterior major】, the 【125†Obliquus superior】, and the 【126†Obliquus inferior】. The first cervical or 【127†suboccipital nerve】 lies between the artery and the 【128†posterior arch】 of the atlas.
L173:   * Segments of vertebral artery lateral projection The fourth (intradural or intracranial) part pierces the 【129†dura mater】 and inclines medially to the front of the 【130†medulla oblongata】; it is placed between the 【131†hypoglossal nerve】 and the anterior root of the first cervical nerve and beneath the first digitation of the 【132†ligamentum denticulatum】. In the midline at the 【108†medullopontine sulcus】, it merges with the vessel of the opposite side to form the 【72†basilar artery】.
L174: ### Triangle
L175: 
L176: [【133†edit】]
L177: 
L178: Triangle of the vertebral artery is a region within the root of the neck and has following boundaries:^{【134†[5]】}
L179: 
L180:   * Medial border of 【135†anterior scalene muscle】 (lateral)
L181:   * Lateral border of 【113†longus colli muscle】 (medial)
L182:   * Carotid tubercle (apex)
L183:   * First part of 【73†subclavian artery】 (base)
L184: 
L185: The vertebral artery runs from base to apex (prior to entering the transverse foramen of 6th cervical vertebra).
L186: The carotid tubercle separates the vertebral artery which passes directly behind it from the common carotid artery which lies directly in front of it. The ideal site for palpating the carotid pulse is to gently press the 【136†common carotid artery】 against the carotid tubercle.^{【137†[6]】}
L187: ### Variation
L188: 
L189: [【138†edit】]
L190: There is commonly variations in the course and size of the vertebral arteries, usually on both sides artery diameters are asymmetrical.^{【139†[7]】} For example, differences in size between left and right vertebral arteries may range from a slight asymmetry to marked 【140†hypoplasia】 of one side, with studies estimating a prevalence of unilateral vertebral artery hypoplasia between 2% and 25%.^{【141†[8]】} In 3-15% of the population, a bony bridge called the 【142†arcuate foramen】 covers the groove for the vertebral artery on vertebra C1.
L191: Rarely, the vertebral arteries enter the subarachnoid space at C1-C2 (3%) or C2-C3 (only three cases have been reported) vertebral levels instead of the atlanto-occipital level.^{【143†[9]】}
L192: The portion of vertebral arteries located within the skull (intracranial) have diameters of 3.17 mm. The intracranial length for the left vertebral artery (32.4 mm) is longer than the right (31.5 mm). The angle where vertebral arteries meet the 【72†basilar artery】 (vertebrobasilar junction), is 46 degrees.^{【144†[10]】}
L193: #### Vertebral artery dominance
L194: 
L195: [【145†edit】]
L196: 
L197: Vertebral artery dominance (VAD) is typically a normal congenital vascular variation of the vertebral arteries. It refers to the asymmetry of the VA diameters on both sides, with the larger diameter being the dominant side and the smaller diameter being the nondominant side.^{【139†[7]】}
